problemText: Which of the following is a statistical question? Remember: a statistical question is one where you expect the answers to differ from person to person or object to object.
choices: How many languages does the principal of our school speak?
What is the current temperature in our city at this exact moment?
How many grains of sand are on this specific beach right now?
What is the favorite color of each student in our class?
hints: A statistical question asks something of many different people or objects, where separate answers are expected.
Three of these questions have only one correct answer. Which one expects many different answers?

problemText: Maya's teacher asks her to collect data about snack preferences. Maya writes: 'What is the favorite snack of our school?' Is this a statistical question? Explain why or why not.
choices: No, because even though many students are in the school, the question only produces one answer total for the whole school.
Yes, because the question mentions a large group (the whole school) and large groups always lead to multiple different answers.
Yes, because each student in the school will answer the question separately, giving many different responses that vary from person to person.
No, because the question asks 'what is the favorite snack' meaning it seeks one single favorite rather than collecting separate answers from each student.
hints: Use the variability test: would each member of the school give a separate, different answer, or does the question ask for just one number for the whole group?
Mentioning a group is not enough by itself. Count how many final answers the question would produce.

problemText: A coach observes his track team during practice. He wants to turn this question into a statistical question: 'How fast did the runner complete the 100-meter race?' Which rewrite would make it statistical?
choices: How fast did the fastest runner on the team complete the 100-meter race?
How fast did each member of the team complete the 100-meter race?
How fast should runners on the team try to complete the 100-meter race?
How did the team's average speed compare to other schools' speeds?
hints: To make a question statistical, change it so that each member of a group can give a separate, possibly different answer.
The original question names one runner. What change would let every team member answer separately?

problemText: A student reads these two questions and claims they are both statistical questions: (1) 'How many siblings does each student in our grade have?' and (2) 'How many siblings do all the students in our grade have combined?' Apply the variability test to both questions. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both are statistical because they both ask about students in our grade and require data collection from the group.
Only Question 2 is statistical because combining information from many students automatically makes a question statistical.
Only Question 1 is statistical because each student can give a different answer, while Question 2 has only one combined total.
Neither is statistical because the answer depends on family information rather than classroom characteristics.
hints: For each question, ask: would the answers differ from student to student, or would there be only one final number?
A statistical question needs each member of the group to give a separate, possibly different answer. Which question structure allows that?

problemText: Jordan wants to research how students in his school spend their free time after school. He starts with this question: 'What do students do after school?' Explain what is wrong with this question, and then rewrite it so that it becomes a statistical question.
choices: The question is too vague. Rewrite it as: 'What is the most common thing that students do after school?'
The question is incomplete because it does not specify which school. Rewrite it as: 'What do students in middle schools do after school?'
The question is wrong because free time is too personal. Rewrite it as: 'Do students prefer indoor or outdoor activities after school?'

The question is too vague and does not clearly show that each student should give a separate answer. Rewrite it as: 'How many hours does each student in our school spend on free time activities after school?'
hints: A statistical question must be specific enough that different students can give separate, measurable answers. What makes the original question unclear about this?
When you rewrite, think about the lesson tip: change who or what the question asks about so every member of a group can answer separately.

problemText: A student analyzing four questions decides that exactly two of them are statistical: (A) 'How old is our class pet?' (B) 'How much does each student in our class weigh?' (C) 'What is the total cost of all the books in our school library?' (D) 'How many hours of video games do the students in our class play each week?' Apply the variability test to all four questions. Which pair did the student correctly identify as statistical?
choices: A and B
B and D
C and D
A and C
hints: For each question, test whether you expect one single answer or many different answers. Do not just count how many people or things the question mentions.
Remember: even if a question talks about a group, it is not statistical if it only produces one final number for that whole group. Check questions C and D carefully.

problemText: A dot plot shows data on a number line where each value in a data set gets its own dot. What happens when the same value appears more than once in the data set?
choices: The dots are stacked directly on top of each other above that value.
The dots are placed side by side horizontally next to each other.
Only one dot is drawn, no matter how many times the value appears.
The value is combined with nearby values and shown as a single mark.
hints: Think about what happens to multiple pets at the same number on Ms. Rivera's plot.
The key word is 'stack'—dots are placed vertically, not horizontally.

problemText: A teacher collects data on the number of books read by 8 students: 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 4. If this data is displayed as a dot plot, how many dots would be stacked above the value 2?
choices: 2 dots
3 dots
4 dots
8 dots
hints: Count how many times the value 2 appears in the list.
Remember that each occurrence of 2 gets its own dot, stacked above that value.

problemText: A histogram displays data with intervals that are all the same width. Why do the bars in a histogram sit directly next to each other with no gaps between them?
choices: Because gaps would make the histogram look cluttered and interrupt the visual flow showing how data is distributed across intervals.
Because histograms must follow a formatting rule that distinguishes them from other graph types used in mathematics and statistics.
Because each value belongs to exactly one interval, and the bars represent consecutive, non-overlapping intervals.
Because the number line must be completely filled to show all possible values without leaving any empty space.
hints: Think about what happens if two intervals overlap or if there is a gap between them.
Every single data value needs to fit into exactly one interval—no value can be counted twice or left out.

problemText: A coach collects data from 25 players on how many goals they scored. The values range from 3 goals all the way to 48 goals, and most players scored a different number. The coach wants to display this data on a single page that is easy to read. Should the coach use a dot plot or a histogram, and what is the main reason?
choices: A dot plot, because it can display any amount of data and makes every individual score visible so nothing gets hidden in intervals.
A histogram, because histograms are more professional and work for any data set no matter the size.
A dot plot, because 25 values is a small data set and small data sets always use dot plots.
A histogram, because there are many values spread across a wide range, and grouping them into intervals keeps the display readable.
hints: Look at the size of the data set (25) and how spread out the values are (3 to 48).
Compare this situation to Mr. Okafor's 20 homework-minutes data—what made a histogram a good choice there?

problemText: A histogram shows how many hours 16 students spent studying for a test. The intervals are 0-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-11 hours. The bars have heights of 4, 6, 4, and 2 respectively. A student looks at the bar above the 6-8 interval and says, 'This bar tells me that 4 students studied for exactly 7 hours.' Why is this statement incorrect?
choices: Because the bar only tells us that 4 students studied somewhere between 6 and 8 hours, not that all of them studied exactly 7 hours.
Because the interval 6-8 contains more than 4 specific values that could be scored, so grouping them loses information about which exact values actually occurred.
Because histograms record frequencies in ranges rather than exact measurements, and 4 students somewhere in that interval could have studied 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, or 8 hours separately.
Because the bar height represents a frequency count across an entire interval, not the number of students who chose one particular value within that range.
hints: Think about what is lost when individual values are grouped into an interval.
A histogram groups data together for readability—what exact information is no longer visible once values are grouped?

problemText: A teacher displays student test scores on a histogram with equal intervals: 60-69, 70-79, 80-89, and 90-99. The bar heights are 3, 7, 8, and 2 respectively. The teacher then decides to create a dot plot of the same data. What would be a valid concern about making this switch from a histogram to a dot plot?
choices: A dot plot cannot show scores in the 60-69 range because those are too low to measure accurately.
The dot plot would need 20 dots spread across 40 possible exact values, and if students actually scored many different exact scores, the plot could become crowded and hard to read.
A dot plot is not allowed if there are more than 15 data points because the display rules require switching to intervals for larger data sets.
A dot plot would require intervals like the histogram uses, so it would not actually simplify or improve the way the data is shown to viewers.
hints: Count the total number of data values represented by the histogram bars.
Think about how many different exact scores the students could have—if spread across a wide range with many different values, what happens to readability on a dot plot?

problemText: Four students scored 78, 82, 85, and 89 on a quiz. What is the mean score?
hints: Add all four scores together first.
Then divide your total by how many students took the quiz.

problemText: A student ordered the heights of five classmates from shortest to tallest: 52 inches, 54 inches, 56 inches, 59 inches, 61 inches. What is the median height?
choices: 54 inches
57.6 inches
56 inches
59 inches
hints: The median is the middle value when the data is already in order.
With five values, count to find which one sits exactly in the middle.

problemText: Six students recorded the number of books they read last month: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6. Since there is an even number of values, which two numbers should you use to find the median?
choices: 2 and 6
3 and 4
3 and 5
4 and 5
hints: With six values, the two middle ones are in positions 3 and 4 when counted from left to right.
Find the two values that sit in the exact middle of your ordered list.

problemText: A teacher measured the times, in seconds, that eight students held their breath: 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 25, 27, 58. One student held their breath much longer than everyone else. Calculate both the mean and the median, then explain why one measure better describes a typical hold time for this group.
choices: Mean is 26.75 seconds; median is 22.5 seconds. The median is better because the 58-second outlier pulls the mean up away from where most students clustered.
Mean is 28.5 seconds; median is 22.5 seconds. The mean is better because it includes information from the student who held their breath longest.
Mean is 26.75 seconds; median is 23.5 seconds. The mean is better because using the average of all values gives a more complete picture than picking the middle.
Mean is 26.75 seconds; median is 22.5 seconds. Both measures are equally good because they both use data from the same eight students.
hints: Add all eight times and divide by 8 for the mean. Then find the average of the 4th and 5th values for the median.
Think about where the 58-second value pulls the mean, and where most of the actual data sits.

problemText: A soccer team recorded how many goals each of nine players scored in the season: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7. Two students need to report the center of this data set. Jordan says the mean is about 4.4 goals, and Casey says the median is 5 goals. Which student's measure is correct, and why is it still an appropriate choice for describing a typical player's goals?
choices: Only Jordan is correct; the mean always works best when the data is spread evenly across a range.
Both are correct; since there is no outlier pulling the data to one side, both the mean and median land close together and describe the data well.
Only Casey is correct; the median only works when there are no outliers at all in the data.
Both are correct; the median is always more reliable than the mean no matter what the data looks like.
hints: Check whether there is a value far above or far below the rest of the data set.
When no outlier exists, how close together do the mean and median usually sit?

problemText: A store tracks the number of items seven customers bought: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 15. The customer who bought 15 items was stocking up for a charity event. If the manager uses the mean to predict how many items a typical customer will buy next week, what error would she make, and how would using the median instead give a more honest prediction?
choices: The mean would be about 3.7 items, which accurately reflects that seven customers bought a total of 30 items. The median would be 3 items, but medians cannot be used to predict future purchases.
The mean would be about 3.7 items, which is too low because most customers buy more than that. The median would be 3 items, which is also too low, so neither measure works.

The mean would be about 3.7 items, which is too high because the 15-item purchase is an outlier. The median would be 3 items, which sits where most customers actually cluster, so it better predicts a typical purchase.
The mean would be about 5.2 items, which correctly accounts for the one large purchase. The median would be 3 items, which ignores the customer's needs and is therefore unfair.
hints: First, add up all seven values and divide by 7 to find the mean. Then find the middle value when the data is ordered.
Think about what most customers actually bought, and how the 15-item outlier moves the mean away from that typical amount.

problemText: A data set has a minimum value of 8 and a maximum value of 35. What is the range?
hints: Range means the spread from smallest to largest.
Subtract the minimum from the maximum.

problemText: Four students timed how long they could hold a plank: 25 seconds, 18 seconds, 32 seconds, and 20 seconds. Order the data and identify the median of this data set.
choices: 18 seconds
32 seconds
25 seconds
22.5 seconds
hints: Arrange all four times in order from least to greatest first.
With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values.

problemText: The five-number summary for minutes spent on chores is: minimum 10, Q1 = 15, median = 20, Q3 = 28, maximum = 40. Calculate the interquartile range (IQR).
choices: 13 minutes
10 minutes
20 minutes
30 minutes
hints: The IQR is the spread of the middle half of the data.
Subtract Q1 from Q3.

problemText: A teacher recorded test scores for eight students: 62, 71, 78, 81, 85, 88, 92, 96. After ordering the data, what is the value of Q3 (the third quartile)?
hints: Q3 is the median of the upper half of the data.
With 8 values (even count), split at the center without including the middle values themselves in either half.

problemText: Two classes tracked pages read over a month. Class A has a five-number summary of: 5, 20, 50, 80, 120 (pages). Class B has: 5, 40, 50, 60, 120 (pages). Both classes have the same median of 50 pages, yet their data look different. Compute the IQR for each class and explain what the difference tells you.
choices: Class A has an IQR of 115 and Class B has an IQR of 115; both classes are identical.
Class A has an IQR of 60 and Class B has an IQR of 20; Class A's middle half is more tightly bunched.
Class A has an IQR of 60 and Class B has an IQR of 20; Class B's middle half is more tightly bunched.
Class A has an IQR of 60 and Class B has an IQR of 20; the classes have the same spread.
hints: Remember that the center alone can hide the story — the median is the same, but spread matters.
Calculate IQR = Q3 − Q1 for each class, then think about what a smaller IQR means.

problemText: A scientist measured the height (in centimeters) of nine seedlings: 12, 8, 15, 14, 10, 11, 13, 16, 9. One seedling grew unusually tall at 16 cm. Compute the five-number summary, the range, and the IQR. Then explain why the IQR is a better measure of spread than the range for describing the typical spread of these seedlings.
choices: Range is 8 cm, IQR is 3.5 cm; the range is better because it uses all the data values from minimum to maximum and therefore gives the most complete picture of variability.
Range is 8 cm, IQR is 4 cm; the range is always the larger number, and a larger measure of spread is more reliable than a smaller one for describing how the seedlings vary in height.
Range is 8 cm, IQR is 3.5 cm; the range is better because the unusually tall seedling at 16 cm is part of the data and should be counted fully in any measure of how spread out the heights are.
Range is 8 cm, IQR is 3.5 cm; the IQR ignores the one unusually tall seedling and better describes the spread of most of the data.
hints: Order the nine values first: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. The median is the 5th value. For an odd count, exclude it when finding Q1 and Q3.
Think about which measure is affected more by the one very tall seedling at 16 cm.
